summary: For ages 5–7, children classify dinosaurs as plant-eaters (herbivores) or meat-eaters (carnivores) by reading a visible clue on the animal — especially tooth shape (sharp, often serrated blades or points for slicing and tearing flesh; blunt, peg-like, leaf-shaped or flat ridged teeth for stripping, shredding or grinding plants). The core move is classify-WITH-REASON: not just labelling but justifying from an observed feature, with corroborating clues (long neck for reaching foliage; sharp hooked claws on many meat-eaters, though claws alone are not proof because some plant-eaters had big claws too) and a deliberate challenge to the 'big/scary = meat-eater' misconception, since some of the largest dinosaurs were plant-eaters.
misconceptions: 'Big or fierce-looking dinosaurs must be meat-eaters' — the largest dinosaurs were plant-eating long-necks.
'All dinosaurs ate meat' (fed by scary media) — most known dinosaurs were herbivores.
'You can tell diet from size/colour' — the reliable clue is teeth (and jaws), not size.
'Sharp teeth always mean it hunted big animals' — sharp teeth mean meat/flesh, but could be fish or small prey.
'Plant-eaters have no defences' — many had horns, plates, or spikes despite eating plants.

activities.title: Tooth detective: sort and justify
steps: Examine a dinosaur's teeth close-up (zoom/magnify a tooth image): decide whether they are sharp, serrated meat-cutting points or blunt plant-eating teeth (pegs, leaf shapes or flat grinding ridges).
Place the dinosaur into a PLANT-EATER bin or a MEAT-EATER bin.
Say out loud or record WHY: 'blunt or flat teeth strip or grind leaves, so plant-eater' / 'sharp points tear meat, so meat-eater'.

After a correct sort, look at a second clue (long neck for reaching branches, or sharp hooked claws) and check whether it points to the same diet — remembering that claws are only a hint, because some plant-eaters had big claws too.
Optionally use a free-explore mode to flip open and inspect any dinosaur's tooth close-up before committing to a bin.
Meet a 'trap' case: a colossal long-necked dinosaur that looks fierce but has blunt peg-like teeth for stripping leaves (not sharp blades) — decide its diet from the teeth, not its size.
activities.insight: Tooth shape is usually a good clue to diet, and multiple body features can agree; a dinosaur's size or scary appearance does NOT decide what it ate — evidence over first impression.

activities.title: Tooth-rule poster to read first
steps: Study a contrast display of a sharp serrated (steak-knife) tooth beside a flat ridged grinder, each labelled with 'meat' or 'plants'.
Tap or point to example dinosaurs to see which group they belong to and the reason why.
State the rule back in your own words before attempting the sorting activity.
activities.insight: Sharp pointed teeth are for cutting/tearing meat; flat ridged teeth are for grinding plants — a clear rule to apply when sorting.

activities.title: Check the concept: categorise and choose
steps: Sort a set of about four dinosaurs into herbivore and carnivore groups.
Answer: 'Sharp pointed teeth are for…?' (choose: tearing meat / grinding plants).
Name one plant-eating dinosaur and one meat-eating dinosaur.
activities.insight: The child can apply the tooth rule and give examples of each diet group.

activities.title: Fossil-detective talk (optional Socratic variant)
steps: Respond to a prompt such as 'What do the teeth tell you about what this dinosaur ate?'
Explain your reasoning aloud and respond to a follow-up: 'Does being big mean it ate meat?'
activities.insight: Articulating the tooth clue in conversation reinforces reasoning from evidence rather than appearance.

checkQuestion: Here are two dinosaurs: one is huge with a long neck and small flat, blunt teeth; the other is smaller with a big head full of sharp pointed teeth. Which one ate plants and which ate meat? How can you tell from the teeth — and does being BIG mean a dinosaur ate meat?
checkAnswer: The huge long-necked one with flat blunt teeth ate PLANTS (flat teeth grind leaves) — even though it's the biggest. The smaller one with sharp pointed teeth ate MEAT (sharp teeth tear flesh). You tell from tooth shape, not size: being big does NOT mean a dinosaur was a meat-eater — some of the biggest dinosaurs were plant-eaters.
